chapter.p: Whenever any non-trivial and narratively interesting event happens within the game the players should be involved in a check to determine the outcome. For example, a player might make a check to climb a wall, to stab an enemy, close a protective circle, block an attack, cast a spell, resist their fear or heights, or jump a horse over a fence. Alternatively, the players might have to make a countercheck when they are being attacked, when they are suffering from hyperthermia, or to notice when someone is trying to swindle them in a card game.

section.p: All game mechanics in Malleus Deum are based on Checks, which in turn are based on the concept of Actor-Action-Object triplets, a theory used to describe interactions between entities in which an Actor performs an Action upon an Object. In Malleus Deum, we decompose each Action into a Check made by the Actor, and an opposing Countercheck, made by the Object.

playexample.p: When Dourli attacks a goblin with his axe then, Dourli is the Actor and the goblin is the Object. Dourli might attempt to perform this action with an Axe Cleave check and the Goblin might perform a Dodge countercheck.

Subsequently, the goblin may try and stab Dourli with his short sword. Now the goblin is the Actor, Dourli is the Object, and the goblin might use a Sword Strike check while Dourli counters with a Shield Block countercheck.

indexentry.indexdefn: Players make Checks by rolling the dice to determine the outcome of actions in the game.
An Actor-Action-Object triplet is a structure for describing events, where an Actor (entity) performs an Action (verb) on an Object (target).
An Object is the thing upon which an Actor performs an Action. When a PC strikes at a goblin with their sword, the goblin is the object of this action.
Anything that acts upon or may be acted upon in the game, PCs and antagonists, including environmental hazards etc.
An action is the verb being performed by the Actor upon the Object in a Check.

An actor, in the game, is any entity which may act upon another. During combat the Actor is usually the character whose turn it is. When a PC makes a Sword Strike against a goblin, then PC is the actor.

section.p: Making checks involves the following steps outlined below, and then discussed in detail in coming sections:

description.p: The actor decides what they want to try and do, and selects a Check to perform that action.

Before a check can be made the character must satisfy any prerequisites of that check, including having enough time to perform the action and having an appropriate rank in the ability to use the check.

descriptions.term: ii) The Object Chooses a Countercheck

description.p: After the actor decides what check they are using, the object(s) decide which countercheck they will use to oppose that check.
The object must be able to satisfy any prerequisites required by the countercheck including training and time requirements.
The check result is determined by comparing two skill results, the Actor's and the Object's.
Typically, Players involved in the check roll two different colored d20s. The darker die is the Fate die. The lighter die is the Skill die.
Antagonists, usually use a Flat DC for checks and counterchecks.

High and Low values on the Fate die add special tags to the result including Blessed, Righteous, Damned and Cursed, which may be used to trigger other actions and effects. Similarly doubles add the Stars Align tag.
Certain Checks and Counterchecks have a Point Pool cost, which may be affected by the Fate Die, and must be paid now.
The face value on the Skill die is modified by the ability's rank, and modifiers caused by fate, and point pool exhaustion.
Then the resulting Skill of the Actor is compared with the skill of the Object to determine the check's level of success.

descriptions.description: Any triggered interrupts may be performed now.
The effects of the Check are applied based on the level of success of the check's description.
Any triggered retorts may be performed now.

section.p: First the Actor decides what they want to do, and then they choose a Viable Check that allows them to do that.

subsection.p: The Actor needs to make a declaration about what check they are taking so that the Objects can choose a countercheck.
Most of the time the choice of which check to use should be fairly straightforward, to jump a horse over a fence you would make a check using the Riding ability, you swim using the Swim ability.

However, some negotiation between the GM and the player might be necessary to choose the most appropriate check to perform for a given action, and whether the prerequisites for that action are met, to choose which Recall Knowledge Lore check to use from multiple Lore abilities, or to ask about range or reach of weapons, cover and so on.

When the choiec of Check is not clear use the following rules of thumb:
Use the check that is most specific to the task at hand. The less relevant an ability is to a task the harder the check should be to perform that task. If there is one ability specifically for performing the task at hand, use that ability. For example, when climbing use the Climb ability.
When the GM deems that there is some overlap between abilities then the player may choose whichever ability they prefer, and the GM should apply shifts/modifiers to the Check to reflect the appropriateness of the ability to the current task. For example when trying to recall information about a nobles lineage, one character might make a check using History, while another might use Lore/Heraldry

indexentry.indexdefn: Viable Checks are checks that a character is allowed to perform. A check is viable if it satisfies a number of prerequisites that include having the time required to perform the action, having the required training to perform that action, having points towards any Pool Cost for the check, and any other prerequisites required for the check, within reach for melee attacks.

subsection.p:
A Viable Check satisfies the following prerequisites:
The Actor must have any required Training for the Ability, though some abilities can be used untrained.
The Actor must have time to perform the action. They must pay the Action Point Cost to perform the action.
If the Check has a Point Pool Cost then that Pool must not be empty, In order to cast a spell which has a Magic Pool Cost the character's magic pool must be greater than zero.
The Actor must satisfy any other prerequistes specifically for that check, :
wielding a sword to use Sword Strike,
object within reach for melee attacks,
object within range for ranged attacks,
and any other requirments listed in the check description

subsubsection.p: By default checks require that the character have training in order to perform any checks associated with the ability, the character must have ranks in the ability to use it.
Many abilities may be used without training. Abilities with an Untrained value or a minimum rank of 0 do not require training to perform checks.

subsection.subsubsection:
Pay Action Point Cost
In order to perform an action a character must have enough time available to do so.
Outside of combat the rules deal with time informally. So it is up to the GM to determine how long a check will take, which might be in minutes, hours or days.
During combat time is broken into 6 second Rounds. Characters get one Turn each round, and each turn is broken down into 5 Action Points (APs). The character can spend these action points to perform actions. If a character does not have the APs to perform a check they may not even attempt to perform that check.
Action Points (APs)
Combat time is broken down into 10 second rounds. During each round every combatant gets one turn.

Combat time is broken down into 10 second rounds. During each round every combatant gets one turn.

section.p: Once the Actor has chosen a check, the Object chooses a Viable Countercheck. For example, if the actor makes a physical-attack the object has to choose one from a number of different physical-defence counterchecks, Armour, Dodge, Shield Block, or Parry.

A Countercheck is Viable in the same sense as a Check is, except that instead of having an AP Cost, Counter Checks are usually free or have a Reaction cost, that is they require that the object spend their Out-of-Turn Action.

subsection.p:
A Viable Countercheck satisfies the following conditions:
The Object must have any required Training for the Ability, though some abilities can be used untrained.
The Object must have an unused OOTA if their countercheck requires one.
If the Countercheck has a Point Pool Cost then then that Pool must not be empty.
The Actor must satisfy any other prerequistes specifically for that countercheck, :
wielding a sword to use Sword Parry,
and any other requirments listed in the check description

indexentry.indexdefn: During each round every combatant gets one Out Of Turn Action that they can spend once to perform a certain of checks outside of their turn.
During each round every combatant gets one Out Of Turn Action that they can spend once to perform a certain checks outside of their turn.
Reactions are Out of Turn Actions used to make certain Counter Checks.
Are Out-of-Turn Actions that occur before any results of a check are applied.
Are Out-of-Turn Actions that occur after any results of a check are applied.

subsection.p: Some counterchecks require the use of a Reaction, which is a type of Out-of-Turn Action. In order to perform those Counterchecks the character must spend their Out-of-Turn Action. If they have already spent their Out-of-Turn action this round then they cannot perform Counterchecks that use a Reaction.

section.p: The success or failure of an action is determined by comparing the Skill of the Actor and the Object. There are a number of ways to evaluate the Skill. However, in most circumstances, the Players Roll Dice and the Antagonists use Static Check Values:
section.subsection:
Roll Dice
Roll two different coloured d20s. The face value of the dark die is the Fate Value. The face value of the lighter die is the Initial Skill Value or simpley their Initial Skill .
The Skill is the sum of the Initial Skill, the characters ability rank and any shifts that apply, Dourli makes an Axe Strike III attack, he rolls a 13 adds 3 for his rank to get a Skill of 16.
For example, suppose Dourli rolls a 12 on his Skill Die while attacking with his Axe Strike III ability. The attack has no modifiers, there are no shifts. Then the Skill for that attack is 12 + 3 = 15.
Later, Dourli rolls a 15 on his Skill Die while attacking the same Goblin with his Dagger Strike II ability. Unfortunately that goblin has ducked behind a small wall and the GM decides that this cover gives the attack two shifts down. Then the Skill for that attack is 15 + 2 - 4 = 13.
{% include "docs/sidebars/shifts.xml" %}

subsection.p: When the GM wants the players to remain uncertain about whether they have succeeded against an antagonist he can do a Hidden Roll. This only applies to PVE checks, checks with a PC versus an antagonist. Here the GM rolls a hidden Skill die for the anatagonist and adds the antagonists Ability Rank to the result. This skill value is unmodified by criticals or fate. The skill result is not disclosed to the players.
For Hidden Checks the antagonist borrows Fate as usual for the purposes of triggering out of turn actions.

playexample.p: Dourli attempts to decieve, Emrich, the head of the local thieves guild and the GM does not want Dourli to know whether he succeeded or not. Dourli checks his Deception, and gets a Skill of 18. Emrich's Perception has a rank of 4. The GM rolls a hidden d20 for skill. He rolls a 15 and adds Emrich's rank of 4 for a hidden skill result of 19. The GM does not tell Dourli this result. Dourli is left thinking that he probably succeeded, but he is not entirely sure.

subsection.p: Sometimes the GM does not even want the players to know they are making a check, Passive Perception checks may be made to have characters notice something about their environment without them asking to make the check. In this case we use Passive Checks.

A Passive Check is basically a combination of a Static Check and a Hidden Check. Here the GM calculates a static DC for the PC by adding the PCs rank in an ability to 10, and then rolls a hidden check for the antagonist against that DC. No Fate is used. The GM should remember that PCs always win draws against an antagonist.

indexentry.indexdefn: Occurs when the face value of the d20 die is 1, before any modifiers, shifts or other adjustments.
Occurs when the face value of the d20 die is 20, before any modifiers, shifts or other adjustments.

section.p: To resolve the Fate Outcome check the face value of the Fate Die:

olist.li: A Natural 20 is Blessed and Lucky. The player gains the Blessings of Mithras boon.
A Natural 1 is Cursed and Damned. The player suffers Ill Omens bane.

section.p: If the Fate Die and Skill Die have the same Face Value, Doubles, then the Stars Align which trigger further actions.
The various fate results can trigger OOTAs for you, your allies and the NPCs. In addition, the fate values affect the Pool Point cost of checks as follows:

subsubsection.p: When the player rolls a Natural 20 on their Fate die they perform the Blessings of Mithras the player may choose one of the following boons:

descriptions.description: Halve the pool cost of the check or reduce the cost to zero if the cost is one.
Shift the Skill result up twice.
If this action is performed during a characters turn in combat then this check is free and requires no action points. If this action is a combat OOTA then it is free.

subsubsection.p: When Ill Omens occur the player must apply the first of the effects, that is applicable to the check, in the following list:

descriptions.description: If the check has an associated pool then increase the Pool Cost by one. If the check does not have an associated pool then this effect does not apply.
If the player has remaining action points after paying for this check then those points are lost. If the character does not have any remaining APs after this action then this effect does not apply.
Shift the Skill Die result down twice.

indexentry.indexdefn: Rolling doubles on a check adds the Stars-Align tag to the result.

subsubsection.p: Doubles gain the Stars Align tag which may trigger Out-of-Turn Actions.

Point Pool Cost
Check Point Pool Cost
Check Cost
Cost
Some checks have a cost in points that the character must pay from one of their point pools in order to make a check, casting spells usually costs points from the Magic Pool. You can tell if an action has an associated Point Pool by checking whether it has a Pool Cost or if it uses one the Point Pool keywords, Magic Pool. Checks made with those abilities may deduct the cost from the point pool, see Tabletable:point-pool-checks on pagetable:point-pool-checks.
subsection.subsubsection:
Exhaustion
{% include "docs/tables/exhaustion_table.xml" %}
If the point pool would be reduced below zero, then instead:
The pool value becomes zero, and
Shift the skill die down twice, and
Roll on the exhaustion table for that pool.
If the pool cost for a check is zero then performing the action usually has a negligable effect on the associated point pool. However the cost can still be affected by Fate and perhaps other factors.

section.p: Any interupts that are triggered happen now. Interrupts are OOTAs that occur before the triggering action. Interrupts count as OOTAs towards the action economy and in order to perform one a character has to spend their unused OOTA for the turn.
If an interrupt occurs and after the interrupt occurs the preconditions for the initial check are no longer met then the initial check automatically fails.

chapter.section:
Resolve Check using Skill
Once the Skill values have been determined for the Actor and the Object we can compare them to find the outcome of the check as follows:
Actor Skill = Objects Skill
then the result is Tied. If a check occurs between a PC and an Antagonist, then the PC always succeeds on a tie, because the PCs are heroes; even if the PC is the Object of the check. In all other cases the Actor succeeds on a Tie, during PVP checks.
Actors Skill Objects Skill then the result is a Success Actors Skill Objects Skill + 5 is both a Righteous Success and a Success. Actors Skill Objects Skill is a Fail Actors Skill Objects Skill + 10 is a Critical Success. Actors Skill Objects Skill - 10 a Critical Fail and a Fail.
Note when interpreting these results a Critical Success is also considered to be a Righteous Success, a Righteous Success is also considered to be a Success, and a Critical Failure is also considered to be a Failure.
See Tabletable:check-dcs which shows probabilities of success for checks on pagetable:check-dcs.

section.p: Retorts happen now in reverse initiative order.
This section contains some extra details about using checks.

subsection.p: The GM should usually only require players to check when: the outcome is uncertain and failure would make the game more interesting .

Many tasks are easy enough that they can be completed automatically. In this case no check is required. Harder variants of the task might require a check though. For example, opening a door might be considered an easy task that automatically succeeds, while opening a door quietly might require a check. Similarly breaking down a door might require a check to perform quickly but can be done automatically given enough time, and that one of the characters carries an axe.
A problem arises that players will at times want to repeat checks until they succeed. We outline some strategies to deal with his.

In the usual course of play each character can perform a check once - twice if a reroll is used. For example, Dourli might try opening a box quickly by picking locks. If Dourli fails he might check to open the box with his axe but he can't try picking the lock again.

subsubsection.p: If the character will definitely succeed after making repeated attempts at a check and there is no other cost then just allow them to succeed, a character who can pick locks tries to open a cheap locked box that they have brought back to their base. In this case the GM should perhaps not have required a check at all. We call this approach Taking Time and if the GM thinks it is reasonable they should allow characters to announce they are Taking Time to perform a task.

subsubsection.subsubsectiontitle: Failure is Success with a Cost
subsubsection.p: If the player fails, they still succeed at the action, but with a "but", Yes, you find the secret door, but the noise attracts a guard, or Yes, you find the secret door, but it takes you so much time that the person you are chasing has fled, or Yes, you open the locked box but you break the lock, or you break your pick.
Each attempt has a cost associated with it. That cost might be time, money or increasing danger ( roll for random encounters at different times).

subsection.p: The most common form of check are Individual Checks, where the character performing the action makes the check. However, sometimes checks have to be made by a group of characters. In Malleus Deum there are two ways of doing this: Everyone Checks and Delegate Checks.

subsubsection.p: Sometimes everyone in a group has to make a check. For example, if the party is attacked using poisonous gas everyone in the group has to make a check to save individually. When Everyone Checks, each group member makes a separate check independent of the rest of the group and each individual suffers any repercussions separately if they fail.

In a delegate check one player character is delegated by the GM to make a check on behalf of the whole group. If that check fails then the whole group fails the check. The GM may choose the delegate at random or at their own discretion. Some examples of Delegate Checks are Initiative, Stealth, Perception, Ambush and Surprise rolls. But more on these later.

subsection.p:
Sometimes the players will get a chance to Reroll a Check. There are a number of rules about rerolling:
No check can be rerolled more than once for any reason
When rerolling all dice used to determine the initial result must be rerolled.
If the player rerolls the check they must take the result from the second roll.
Assume that all checks are able to be rerolled unless the ability states otherwise. Luck based checks cannot be rerolled.

indexentry.indexdefn: When taking fractional values always round up.
When taking fractional values always round up.

subsection.p: Some rules require numeric values to be halved, quartered and so on. When rounding the rule is always round up, half of 7 is 4, and a quarter of 7 is 2.

Advantage Disadvantage Some checks allow players to make checks at Advantage or at Disadvantage. In these cases an additional skill die is rolled (only one Fate die is rolled in this case). When making a check with Advantage the player chooses the higher face value on the two skill dice as the Initial Skill Value. When making a check with Disadvantage the player chooses the lowest face value on the two skill dice as the Initial Skill Value.

In Malleus Deum all rules are optional, but some rules are more optional than others. Rules denoted by the dagger symbol are optional and may or may not be used as the GM prefers, trading off complexity and complications for speed of game play.
